items.title: GhostBat Android Malware Targets 60 Banking and Payment Apps in India
items.summary: A recent investigation uncovered an updated version of GhostBat, an Android malware family targeting 60 banking and payment applications in India. Spread through fraudulent government-service messages and malicious app downloads, GhostBat exploits Android Accessibility Services to steal payment PINs, intercept SMS messages, and collect sensitive data. Researchers identified a transparent overlay technique that captures PIN entries as victims interact with legitimate banking apps, making the attack difficult to recognize. Encrypted loaders and remotely configurable settings further complicate detection. The findings highlight how attackers are advancing mobile banking fraud through increasingly sophisticated techniques designed to evade detection and compromise financial transactions.

items.title: Inside Coruna and DarkSword Chains: From Web Lures to iOS Exploitation
items.summary:
Executive Summary

Seven months after Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published its initial analysis of the Coruna iOS exploit framework, the campaign has continued to evolve: the recovered infrastructure now deploys two distinct exploit chains conditioned on the target device's operating system version. Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework (exhibiting byte-identical JavaScript payloads across multiple recovered configurations). Conversely, devices running later iOS builds receive a DarkSword-derived execution chain. Through October 2026, zLabs identified 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code, with recovered configurations across 93 of these sites mapping to 21 distinct tracking collectors. The analyzed distribution footprint spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and—in several instances—compromised legitimate sites serving the kit via hidden iframes.

This report details our technical analysis of these infrastructure and payload developments. Specifically, we recovered and analyzed both components of the Coruna framework: the client-side JavaScript responsible for environment profiling and exploit chain selection, and the post-escape native payload modules engineered to operate beyond the WebContent sandbox.

What stands out to us:

  • No app install, no user consent. The attack begins inside a web page. A visitor taps a link, the page renders normally, and a hidden frame loads the exploit chain. Later stages fetch native code without ever prompting the user to install anything. There is no App Store review to fail, no configuration profile to accept, no permission dialog to dismiss. From the target's point of view, the page can appear normal.
  • One codebase, many variants. The lures are disposable; the kit is not. Across multiple sites we found the same core JavaScript runtime — byte-for-byte identical in its decoded form — behind wildly different themes, campaign labels, and tracking servers. Defenders who hunt for lure content or a campaign string may miss related sites. Defenders who hunt for the runtime can connect related sites.
  • Native capability that reaches well past the browser. The recovered modules contain kernel memory read and write routines, code that manipulates Apple Mobile File Integrity (AMFI) state, process-memory reads via task ports, application-state monitoring, encrypted C2 communication with certificate validation disabled, and routines that delete crash logs and Safari website-data records.
  • Delivery has already escaped the attacker's own infrastructure. SafeDep independently found matching Coruna code inside a compromised npm package, art-template. That means a site can serve Coruna to its visitors without anyone on the operator's side ever registering a lure domain — the kit arrives through the victim site's own dependency tree.



Fig.1: Selected milestones in Coruna activity and public reporting, February 2025–October 2026. Sources: GTIG, SafeDep and zLabs.

items.title: DHS Order Barring DeepSeek AI Use by Federal Government Agencies
items.summary:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) upped the ante for AI Governance by issuing an order, published in the Federal Register on October 20, 2026, barring the use of DeepSeek Products by US Federal agencies and their employees.

Titled “Notice of Order Regarding Exclusion and Removal of DeepSeek Products from Federal Civilian Executive Branch Information Technology Systems and Procurements,” the order bans the inclusion of DeepSeek AI technology in federal civilian agency purchases and requires removal of DeepSeek products from use, as well as removal of any IT products using DeepSeek technology.

items.title: Beyond the Sandbox: Leveraging Android Intrusion Logs to Expose Advanced Threats
items.summary:
Executive Summary

Some of the most important activity on a compromised Android device occurs when a threat attempts to move beyond the normal application sandbox: an unexpected process starts, a shell is opened, or a binary is staged outside the application’s lifecycle. Understanding those activities requires a multi-layered detection strategy, correlating trusted on-device operating-system telemetry with comprehensive real-time, run-time device, application, network, and phishing analysis.

Android provides that visibility through complementary security and network logging capabilities. For managed devices, Delegated Scope allows an enterprise to grant a specialized security application access to security logs without transferring broader device-management authority. Zimperium Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) has supported this model since Security Logging became available through Delegated Scope, working with our MDM integration partners to help enterprises use these signals for advanced detection and analysis.

Android’s new Intrusion Logging capability extends this value to another important group: users of supported devices who can now choose to collect and securely share similar security, DNS, and connection evidence through Advanced Protection. The objective is consistent—preserve high-value, OS-generated context so defenders can better understand what happened on a device regardless if it is a BYOD or Enterprise managed device.

items.title: QR Codes and Fake AI Tools Expand Mobile Attack Opportunities
items.summary: A recent threat report highlights how attackers are using QR codes and fraudulent AI tools to evade traditional security controls and reach users across devices. Researchers observed campaigns embedding malicious links in QR codes, requiring users to scan them with smartphones and shifting attacks from protected computers to mobile environments. Other campaigns used fake AI-related tools and services to distribute malware and steal sensitive information. These tactics demonstrate how attackers continue to adapt social engineering techniques to emerging technology and cross-device workflows, reinforcing the need for mobile phishing protection, user awareness, and continuous monitoring for suspicious activity.
